description: I am a masters student looking forward to work on space exploration topics
summary:
Sons of Ares is an interactive 3D story that introduces middle schoolers to the robots NASA has left on Mars. Kids watch a launch from Cape Canaveral, follow the trip to Mars, and see where eight robots landed: Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity. Each robot has a story card, a short “How it worked” walkthrough of its engineering, and links to NASA sources. A narrated tour shows Sojourner’s landing and the regions of Mars, such as the Tharsis volcanoes and Valles Marineris. Kids can then speak or type questions, and each robot answers in its own voice.
It answers the challenge by turning dense mission records into a personal story: how each machine worked, what science it made possible, and why it went silent. Most students only hear about active missions. We want them to feel a connection to the explorers that paved the way, so the next generation sees the science behind today’s missions.
details:
What it does: Sons of Ares is a web app where kids explore the robots NASA left on Mars. In Earth mode they see the Cape Canaveral launch site and a glowing trajectory arc. In Mars mode a 3D globe shows eight landing sites: Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity. Each robot has a card with its landing site, coordinates, dates, how long it worked, what it discovered, why it stopped, a fun fact, a three-step “How it worked” walkthrough, and links to NASA sources. A Regions toggle marks Tharsis, Valles Marineris, Hellas, Elysium and the lowlands and highlands. Story mode runs a narrated tour with an animated landing of Sojourner, the first rover on Mars.

Ask a robot: Kids can speak or type a question and hear the robot answer in its own voice. Each answer is grounded in that robot’s verified facts, and the app has built-in answers as a backup.

Benefits and intended impact: Students usually hear about active missions. This shows the history behind them and connects the engineering to the science. Every robot lasted a different length of time and ended for a different reason, so the stories teach about solar power, dust, airbag landings and engineering limits through characters kids care about. We want students to feel a personal link to these explorers and to leave curious about today’s missions.

Tools: React and Vite for the interface, globe.gl (built on Three.js) for the 3D globe, Cloudflare Pages and Pages Functions for hosting and the server side, Cloudflare Workers AI (a Llama model) for the robots’ answers, and the browser’s Web Speech API for voice input and output. Data and images come from NASA mission pages, NSSDCA, the NASA Image and Video Library, and USGS and MOLA maps.

Creativity: The robots are narrators, not subjects. The story follows one journey from launch to landing to meeting each robot, and kids can interrupt it and ask questions out loud.

What we considered: Our audience is ages 11 to 14, so the text is short, the captions are large, and the app can be used by voice or keyboard. Accuracy mattered, so each card links to its NASA source and the chat only draws on those card facts. The app works without AI or a microphone, using typed questions and built-in answers. We plan to add the Moon, with Apollo descent stages, lunar rovers and science stations, next.
